The scoreboard shows the complete sequence of points scored by each player in each of the 10 rounds of the game. It turns out that Caitlin has scored at least as many points in total as Donal after every round of the game. Prove the number of possible scoreboards is divisible by 4 but not by 8.

ie.2026.0.2.reviewed_statement: Find (with proof) all positive integer solutions to the equation $$2^a+2^b+2^c+2^d=60\cdot\min\{a,b,c,d\},$$ where $\min\{a,b,c,d\}$ is the minimum of the numbers $a,b,c,d$.

ie.2026.0.3.reviewed_statement:
Triangle $ABC$ is such that $|AB|>|AC|$ and $\angle BAC=60^\circ$. The circumcentre of triangle $ABC$ is $O$. The angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ meets $BC$ at $D$.

Prove that $\angle ADO=2\angle DAO$.

ie.2026.0.4.reviewed_statement:
Starting from a positive integer $n$, we perform any sequence of operations from the following list:

$A$: If the number is even, we can divide it by $2$.

$B$: We can place the digit $0$ at the end of the number.

$C$: We can place the digit $8$ at the end of the number.

For example, starting with $n=8$, we can obtain the number $90$ by performing the sequence of operations $AAACAB$, as follows: $$8\xrightarrow{A}4\xrightarrow{A}2\xrightarrow{A}1\xrightarrow{C}18\xrightarrow{A}9\xrightarrow{B}90.$$ (a) Prove that the number $2026$ can be obtained starting from $8$.

(b) Can any positive integer $n$ be obtained starting from $8$?

ie.2026.0.5.scope: Full statement compared with the Irish Mathematical Olympiad Compendium (problem papers 1988–2026, compiled at UCD by the IrMO organisers), text layer and page image; figures cropped from the compendium where the statement refers to one.
ie.2026.0.5.reviewed_statement:
For each positive integer $n$, consider $3n$ distinct points on a circle, labelled in clockwise order $1,2,\dots,3n$. An $n$-triangle configuration is a way to split these $3n$ points into $n$ sets of $3$ points each, and connect the $3$ points in each set to form a triangle, such that no two of the $n$ triangles intersect.

Let $S(n)$ be the number of all possible $n$-triangle configurations. For example, $S(1)=1$ because there are only three points, and $S(2)=3$ corresponding to the three configurations $\{123,456\}$, $\{234,561\}$ and $\{345,612\}$.

Find all positive integers $n$ for which $S(n)$ is not a multiple of $3$.

ie.2026.0.6.scope: Full statement compared with the Irish Mathematical Olympiad Compendium (problem papers 1988–2026, compiled at UCD by the IrMO organisers), text layer and page image; figures cropped from the compendium where the statement refers to one.
ie.2026.0.6.reviewed_statement:
Aisling and Brendan play the following game with $2026$ stones.

• Aisling divides the $2026$ stones into three non-empty piles.

• Brendan removes one stone from each of two piles, adds one of those stones to the third pile and discards the remaining stone.

• Aisling and Brendan then continue in turns, starting with Aisling, selecting two piles from which one stone is removed, adding one of those stones to the third pile and discarding the last stone.

• A pile can reduce to zero stones, and stones can be added back to a zero pile, but no pile can become negative.

• The first player unable to move loses the game.

Determine a strategy for Aisling which ensures that she will win the game.

ie.2026.0.9.reviewed_statement: Let $\mathbb{Z}$ denote the set of all integers, $\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ the positive integers (excluding zero), and $c\in\mathbb{Z}$. Find all functions $f:\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\to\mathbb{Z}$ such that for all integers $x>y>0$: $$f(x-y)+f(x+y)=2f(x)+cf(y).$$

ie.2026.0.10.reviewed_statement:
Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with circumcentre $O$. Lines $BO$ and $AC$ intersect at $J$. Lines $CO$ and $AB$ intersect at $L$. The circumcircle of $\triangle BOC$ intersects line $AO$ for the second time at $P$. The circumcircles of $\triangle PCJ$ and $\triangle PBL$ intersect for the second time at $Q$.

Prove that the line $PQ$ passes through the orthocentre $H$ of $\triangle ABC$.

Kazakhstan-rmo-problems.json.coverage_notes: National final grade 11 coverage for 2011–2026: six problems each year except 2020, which has a complete four-problem paper. The 2020 and 2023–2026 papers are common to grades 10–11. Added 2017–2021 statements were read on AoPS and compared with all numbered grade-11 statements in the Matol final-round archive; cross-references expanded and 2018 P2 initial conditions restored as b_0=1 and b_1=2. Official 2025 PDF checks are recorded per problem. Whole-collection source fidelity is not certified. The complete six-problem 2016 grade-11 final was compared with Matol; three AoPS cross-references were expanded, and P3 retains the original curvilinear-triangle specification. Complete six-problem 2014 and 2015 grade-11 finals were compared with Matol; six AoPS cross-references were expanded. The incorrect AoPS 2014 P4 location of N on BC was restored to the original angle-bisector foot on AC. Complete 2011–2013 grade-11 finals were compared with Matol. Six cross-references were expanded. 2012 P2 non-similarity and all 2012 P6 subquestions and positive coefficients were restored. 2013 P6 has an explicit editorial note resolving the intermediate-meeting ambiguity using the archived solution discussion. 1999–2010 grade 11 papers (2 days; 8 problems per year until 2007, 6 from 2008) added from AoPS; unverified. Where AoPS lists a grade 11 problem only as a reference to a grade 9/10 problem (e.g. '10.1'), the referenced text was used.

kz.2025.1.1.reviewed_statement: Find all quadruples $(a,b,c,d)$ of positive integers such that $$2^a+3^b=5^c d,\qquad 2^b+3^a=5^d c.$$
kz.2025.1.1.scope: English statement and all formulas compared with the Russian and Kazakh official final-round original linked from Daryn respa, 2024–2025 archive. P1 natural-number domain restored. No essential statement figure.

kz.2025.1.2.reviewed_statement: Find all strictly increasing functions $f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$ satisfying $$f(mf(n))+f(n)=f(nf(m))+f(m)$$ for all positive integers $m,n$. Here $\mathbb N$ denotes the positive integers.
kz.2025.1.2.scope: English statement and all formulas compared with the Russian and Kazakh official final-round original linked from Daryn respa, 2024–2025 archive. P1 natural-number domain restored. No essential statement figure.

kz.2025.1.3.reviewed_statement: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB\ne AC$, incenter $I$, $A$-excenter $I_A$, altitude $AD$, and circumcircle $\Omega$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of the arc $BAC$ of $\Omega$, and let $AL$ be a diameter of $\Omega$. Put $P=IL\cap I_AD$ and $Q=ID\cap I_AL$. A point $S$ satisfies $SA=SM$ and $SP=SL$. Prove that lines $AP$, $MQ$, and $I_AS$ are concurrent.
kz.2025.1.3.scope: English statement and all formulas compared with the Russian and Kazakh official final-round original linked from Daryn respa, 2024–2025 archive. P1 natural-number domain restored. No essential statement figure.

kz.2025.2.4.reviewed_statement: Let $x,y$ be positive real numbers and $n$ a positive integer such that $$\left\lfloor\frac{x^{n+1}}{y^n}\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor\frac xy\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{y^{n+1}}{x^n}\right\rfloor.$$ Prove that $$-\frac1{2n+1}<x-y<\frac2{2n-1}.$$ Here $\lfloor t\rfloor$ is the greatest integer not exceeding $t$.
kz.2025.2.4.scope: Complete English statements and formulas compared with Russian and Kazakh official final-round original linked from Daryn respa, 2024–2025 archive. Senior P4 also appears as grade 9 P5. P5 angle-bisector endpoints on opposite sides made explicit. No essential statement figures.

kz.2025.2.5.reviewed_statement: Let $ABC$ be a scalene triangle, $M$ the midpoint of $AB$, $I$ its incenter, and $J$ the midpoint of the arc $AB$ of its circumcircle not containing $C$. Tangents $IP$ and $IQ$ are drawn to the circle with centre $J$ and radius $JM$, with $A$ and $P$ on the same side of line $CI$. The circumcircles of $APJ$ and $BQJ$ meet again at $R$. Lines $IP$ and $IQ$ meet line $AB$ at $X$ and $Y$, respectively. The internal angle bisectors from $M$ in triangles $XMJ$ and $YMJ$ meet $XJ$ and $YJ$ at $X_1$ and $Y_1$, respectively. Prove that $X_1$, $Y_1$, and $R$ are collinear.
kz.2025.2.5.scope: Complete English statements and formulas compared with Russian and Kazakh official final-round original linked from Daryn respa, 2024–2025 archive. Senior P4 also appears as grade 9 P5. P5 angle-bisector endpoints on opposite sides made explicit. No essential statement figures.

kz.2025.2.6.reviewed_statement: Let $n,k$ be positive integers with $k+1<2n$. Let $A$ be the set of sequences $(a_1,\ldots,a_{2n})$ such that $a_i\in\{1,-1\}$, $a_1+\cdots+a_{2n}=0$, and $a_1+\cdots+a_i\ge0$ for every $i=1,\ldots,2n$. Let $B=\{a\in A:a_k=1\}$ and $C=\{a\in A:a_{k+1}=1\}$. Prove that $$|B|\,|C|\ge |A|\,|B\cap C|,$$ where $|X|$ denotes the cardinality of $X$.
kz.2025.2.6.scope: Complete English statements and formulas compared with Russian and Kazakh official final-round original linked from Daryn respa, 2024–2025 archive. Senior P4 also appears as grade 9 P5. P5 angle-bisector endpoints on opposite sides made explicit. No essential statement figures.

kz.2013.2.6.reviewed_statement: Two turtles start simultaneously at $(0,0)$. At each step each turtle moves either one unit right or one unit up, from $(x,y)$ to $(x+1,y)$ or $(x,y+1)$. For a positive integer $n$, how many ways can they reach $(n,n)$ without meeting at any intermediate point between departure and arrival?
kz.2013.2.6.text: Editorial clarification: the AoPS and Matol statements say the turtles last met only at (0,0), although both finish at (n,n). The bank explicitly excludes meetings only at intermediate points. This interpretation is supported by the archived Matol solution discussion at https://matol.kz/comments/1028/show, which counts disjoint interior paths between the first and penultimate steps. The supporting discussion is a community solution, not an official wording correction.

nz.2019.0.3.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.

Let $a$, $b$ and $c$ be positive real numbers such that $a + b + c = 3$. Prove that
$$a^a + b^b + c^c \ge 3.$$

nz.2019.0.4.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.
nz.2019.0.4.reviewed_statement: Show that for all positive integers $k$, there exists a positive integer $n$ such that $n2^k - 7$ is a perfect square.

nz.2019.0.5.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.
nz.2019.0.5.reviewed_statement: An equilateral triangle is partitioned into smaller equilateral triangular pieces. Prove that two of the pieces are the same size.

nz.2020.0.1.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.
nz.2020.0.1.reviewed_statement:
Let $P(x) = x^3 - 2x + 1$ and let $Q(x) = x^3 - 4x^2 + 4x - 1$. Show that
$$\text{if } P(r) = 0 \text{ then } Q(r^2) = 0.$$

nz.2020.0.2.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.
nz.2020.0.2.reviewed_statement:
Find the smallest positive integer $N$ satisfying the following three properties.

$N$ leaves a remainder of $5$ when divided by $7$.

$N$ leaves a remainder of $6$ when divided by $8$.

$N$ leaves a remainder of $7$ when divided by $9$.

nz.2020.0.3.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.
nz.2020.0.3.reviewed_statement: There are $13$ marked points on the circumference of a circle with radius $13$. Prove that we can choose three of the marked points which form a triangle with area less than $13$.

nz.2020.0.4.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.
nz.2020.0.4.reviewed_statement: Let $\Gamma_1$ and $\Gamma_2$ be circles internally tangent at point $A$, with $\Gamma_1$ inside $\Gamma_2$. Let $BC$ be a chord of $\Gamma_2$ which is tangent to $\Gamma_1$ at point $D$. Prove that line $AD$ is the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$.

nz.2020.0.5.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.
nz.2020.0.5.reviewed_statement: A sequence of $A$s and $B$s is called antipalindromic if writing it backwards, then turning all the $A$s into $B$s and vice versa, produces the original sequence. For example $ABBAAB$ is antipalindromic. For any sequence of $A$s and $B$s we define the cost of the sequence to be the product of the positions of the $A$s. For example, the string $ABBAAB$ has cost $1 \cdot 4 \cdot 5 = 20$. Find the sum of the costs of all antipalindromic sequences of length $2020$.

Determine the length of the diagonal $BD$.

nz.2021.0.2.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.
nz.2021.0.2.reviewed_statement:
Prove that
$$x^2 + \frac{8}{xy} + y^2 \ge 8$$
for all positive real numbers $x$ and $y$.

Point $C$ lies between $A$ and $B$. Let the circumcircle of triangle $POC$ intersect $\Gamma$ at distinct points $P$ and $Q$. Prove that $\angle AQP = \angle CQB$.

nz.2021.0.5.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.

nz.2022.0.1.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.

Find all integers $a, b$ such that

nz.2022.0.2.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.
nz.2022.0.2.reviewed_statement:
Find all triples $(a, b, c)$ of real numbers such that
$$a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 1 \qquad \text{and} \qquad a(2b - 2a - c) \ge \frac{1}{2}.$$

nz.2022.0.3.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.
nz.2022.0.3.reviewed_statement:
Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a set of $10$ positive integers. Prove that one can find two disjoint subsets $A = \{a_1, \dots, a_k\}$ and $B = \{b_1, \dots, b_k\}$ of $\mathcal{S}$ with $|A| = |B|$ such that the sums
$$x = \frac{1}{a_1} + \dots + \frac{1}{a_k}$$
and
$$y = \frac{1}{b_1} + \dots + \frac{1}{b_k}$$
differ by less than $0.01$; i.e., $|x - y| < 1/100$.

nz.2022.0.4.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.
nz.2022.0.4.reviewed_statement: Triangle $ABC$ is right-angled at $B$ and has incentre $I$. Points $D$, $E$ and $F$ are the points where the incircle of the triangle touches the sides $BC$, $AC$ and $AB$ respectively. Lines $CI$ and $EF$ intersect at point $P$. Lines $DP$ and $AB$ intersect at point $Q$. Prove that $AQ = BF$.

nz.2022.0.5.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.
nz.2022.0.5.reviewed_statement:
The sequence $x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots$ is defined by $x_1 = 2022$ and $x_{n+1} = 7x_n + 5$ for all positive integers $n$. Determine the maximum positive integer $m$ such that
$$\frac{x_n(x_n - 1)(x_n - 2)\dots(x_n - m + 1)}{m!}$$
is never a multiple of $7$ for any positive integer $n$.

nz.2023.0.1.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.
nz.2023.0.1.reviewed_statement:
For any positive integer $n$ let $n! = 1 \times 2 \times 3 \times \dots \times n$. Do there exist infinitely many triples $(p, q, r)$ of positive integers with $p > q > r > 1$ such that the product
$$p! \cdot q! \cdot r!$$
is a perfect square?

nz.2023.0.2.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.
nz.2023.0.2.reviewed_statement: Let $a$, $b$ and $c$ be positive real numbers such that $a + b + c = abc$. Prove that at least one of $a$, $b$ or $c$ is greater than $\frac{17}{10}$.

nz.2023.0.3.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.

nz.2023.0.4.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.

nz.2024.0.4.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.

nz.2025.0.3.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.
nz.2025.0.3.reviewed_statement:
Let $ABC$ be an acute scalene triangle with $AC > BC > AB$. Let the orthocentre be $H$ and circumcentre be $O$. Suppose that lines $BO$ and $CH$ intersect at a point $D$. Point $E$ (where $E \ne C$) lies on side $AC$ so that $OECD$ is cyclic. Point $F$ (where $F \ne C$) lies on side $BC$ such that $CE = FE$. Prove that $BHDF$ is cyclic.

(The orthocentre of a triangle is the point of intersection of its altitudes.)

nz.2025.0.4.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.
nz.2025.0.4.reviewed_statement:
The function $r_n(x)$ is the remainder when $x$ is divided by $n$, where $0 \le r_n(x) < n$. For which $n$ does there exist some ordering $\{a_1, \dots, a_{n-1}\}$ of $\{1, 2, \dots, n-1\}$ such that $\{r_n(a_1), r_n(2 \times a_2), \dots, r_n((n-1) \times a_{n-1})\}$ is an ordering of $\{1, 2, \dots, n-1\}$?

(An ordering of $\{1, 2, \dots, n-1\}$ is the sequence of numbers $1$ to $n-1$ in some order.)

nz.2025.0.5.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.
nz.2025.0.5.reviewed_statement:
Let $a, b, c$ be positive real numbers satisfying $abc = 1$. Determine the smallest possible value of
$$\frac{a^2 + 2025}{a^3(b+c)} + \frac{b^2 + 2025}{b^3(c+a)} + \frac{c^2 + 2025}{c^3(a+b)}.$$

nz.2026.0.1.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.
nz.2026.0.1.reviewed_statement:
Find all positive integers $m$ and $n$ such that
$$\frac{5m + n}{3m + 7n}$$
is a fraction in its simplest form (i.e. it cannot be reduced further).

nz.2026.0.2.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.
nz.2026.0.2.reviewed_statement: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB < AC$. Let $D$ and $E$ be the respective feet of the altitudes from $A$ to $BC$ and $B$ to $AC$, and suppose that $DC = 3 \cdot BD$. Let $X$ be the reflection of point $E$ over line $AD$. Prove that $AXBC$ is cyclic.

nz.2026.0.3.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.
nz.2026.0.3.reviewed_statement:
Do there exist real numbers $x$, $y$ and $z$ satisfying the following?
$$x^4 + (y-2)^2 = y^4 + (z-2)^2 = z^4 + (x-2)^2 = \frac{7}{4}.$$

nz.2026.0.4.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.
nz.2026.0.4.reviewed_statement:
Let $\mathbb{Q}^+$ denote the set of positive rational numbers. Does there exist an infinite subset $\mathcal{S}$ of $\mathbb{Q}^+$ such that every positive rational number is the product of the elements of a unique finite subset of $\mathcal{S}$?

Note: We consider the product of the empty set $\{\}$ to be $1$.

For example, if $\mathcal{S} = \{\frac{1}{2}, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, \dots\}$, then $9$ would be a product of a unique finite subset of $\mathcal{S}$, but not $\frac{15}{2}$, as it can be made by either $\frac{1}{2} \times 15$ or $\frac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 5$.

nz.2026.0.5.scope: Statement fidelity only; solutions not reviewed.
nz.2026.0.5.reviewed_statement: Let $p_i$ denote the $i^{\text{th}}$ odd prime, so $p_1 = 3$, $p_2 = 5$, etc. Does there exist an infinite sequence of positive integers $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ such that for all positive integers $n$, the number $a_1^2 + a_2^2 + \dots + a_n^2$ is a multiple of $p_n$?

uk1.2005.0.1.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2005.0.1.reviewed_statement: Each of Paul and Jenny has a whole number of pounds. He says to her: “If you give me £3, I will have $n$ times as much as you”. She says to him: “If you give me £$n$, I will have $3$ times as much as you”. Given that all these statements are true and that $n$ is a positive integer, what are the possible values for $n$?

uk1.2005.0.2.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2005.0.2.reviewed_statement: Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle, and let $D$, $E$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $A$, $B$ to $BC$, $CA$ respectively. Let $P$ be the point where the line $AD$ meets the semicircle constructed outwardly on $BC$, and $Q$ be the point where the line $BE$ meets the semicircle constructed outwardly on $AC$. Prove that $CP=CQ$.

uk1.2005.0.3.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2005.0.3.reviewed_statement: Determine the least natural number $n$ for which the following result holds: No matter how the elements of the set $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ are coloured red or blue, there are integers $x$, $y$, $z$, $w$ in the set (not necessarily distinct) of the same colour such that $x+y+z=w$.

uk1.2005.0.4.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2005.0.4.reviewed_statement: Determine the least possible value of the largest term in an arithmetic progression of seven distinct primes.

uk1.2005.0.5.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2005.0.5.reviewed_statement:
Let $S$ be a set of rational numbers with the following properties:
i) $\frac12\in S$;
ii) If $x\in S$, then both $\frac{1}{x+1}\in S$ and $\frac{x}{x+1}\in S$.
Prove that $S$ contains all rational numbers in the interval $0<x<1$.

uk1.2006.0.1.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2006.0.1.reviewed_statement: Let $n$ be an integer greater than $6$. Prove that if $n-1$ and $n+1$ are both prime, then $n^2(n^2+16)$ is divisible by $720$. Is the converse true?

uk1.2006.0.2.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2006.0.2.reviewed_statement:
Adrian teaches a class of six pairs of twins. He wishes to set up teams for a quiz, but wants to avoid putting any pair of twins into the same team. Subject to this condition:
i) In how many ways can he split them into two teams of six?
ii) In how many ways can he split them into three teams of four?

uk1.2006.0.3.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2006.0.3.reviewed_statement: In the cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$, the diagonal $AC$ bisects the angle $DAB$. The side $AD$ is extended beyond $D$ to a point $E$. Show that $CE=CA$ if and only if $DE=AB$.

uk1.2006.0.4.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2006.0.4.reviewed_statement: The equilateral triangle $ABC$ has sides of integer length $N$. The triangle is completely divided (by drawing lines parallel to the sides of the triangle) into equilateral triangular cells of side length $1$. A continuous route is chosen, starting inside the cell with vertex $A$ and always crossing from one cell to another through an edge shared by the two cells. No cell is visited more than once. Find, with proof, the greatest number of cells which can be visited.

uk1.2006.0.5.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2006.0.5.reviewed_statement: Let $G$ be a convex quadrilateral. Show that there is a point $X$ in the plane of $G$ with the property that every straight line through $X$ divides $G$ into two regions of equal area if and only if $G$ is a parallelogram.

uk1.2006.0.6.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2006.0.6.reviewed_statement: Let $T$ be a set of $2005$ coplanar points with no three collinear. Show that, for any of the $2005$ points, the number of triangles it lies strictly within, whose vertices are points in $T$, is even.

uk1.2007.0.1.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2007.0.1.reviewed_statement: Find four prime numbers less than $100$ which are factors of $3^{32}-2^{32}$.

uk1.2007.0.2.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2007.0.2.reviewed_statement: In the convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, points $M$, $N$ lie on the side $AB$ such that $AM=MN=NB$, and points $P$, $Q$ lie on the side $CD$ such that $CP=PQ=QD$. Prove that $$\text{Area of }AMCP=\text{Area of }MNPQ=\frac13\,\text{Area of }ABCD.$$

uk1.2007.0.3.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2007.0.3.reviewed_statement: The number $916238457$ is an example of a nine-digit number which contains each of the digits $1$ to $9$ exactly once. It also has the property that the digits $1$ to $5$ occur in their natural order, while the digits $1$ to $6$ do not. How many such numbers are there?

uk1.2007.0.4.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2007.0.4.reviewed_statement: Two touching circles $S$ and $T$ share a common tangent which meets $S$ at $A$ and $T$ at $B$. Let $AP$ be a diameter of $S$ and let the tangent from $P$ to $T$ touch it at $Q$. Show that $AP=PQ$.

uk1.2007.0.5.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2007.0.5.reviewed_statement: For positive real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, prove that $$(a^2+b^2)^2\geq(a+b+c)(a+b-c)(b+c-a)(c+a-b).$$

uk1.2007.0.6.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2007.0.6.reviewed_statement: Let $n$ be an integer. Show that, if $2+2\sqrt{1+12n^2}$ is an integer, then it is a perfect square.

uk1.2008.0.1.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.

uk1.2008.0.2.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2008.0.2.reviewed_statement: Find all solutions in positive integers $x$, $y$, $z$ to the simultaneous equations $$\begin{aligned}x+y-z&=12\\ x^2+y^2-z^2&=12.\end{aligned}$$

uk1.2008.0.3.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2008.0.3.reviewed_statement:
Let $ABC$ be a triangle, with an obtuse angle at $A$. Let $Q$ be a point (other than $A$, $B$ or $C$) on the circumcircle of the triangle, on the same side of chord $BC$ as $A$, and let $P$ be the other end of the diameter through $Q$. Let $V$ and $W$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $Q$ onto $CA$ and $AB$ respectively. Prove that the triangles $PBC$ and $AWV$ are similar.
[Note: the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$ is the circle which passes through the vertices $A$, $B$ and $C$.]

uk1.2008.0.4.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2008.0.4.reviewed_statement: Let $S$ be a subset of the set of numbers $\{1,2,3,\ldots,2008\}$ which consists of $756$ distinct numbers. Show that there are two distinct elements $a$, $b$ of $S$ such that $a+b$ is divisible by $8$.

uk1.2008.0.5.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2008.0.5.reviewed_statement: Let $P$ be an internal point of triangle $ABC$. The line through $P$ parallel to $AB$ meets $BC$ at $L$, the line through $P$ parallel to $BC$ meets $CA$ at $M$, and the line through $P$ parallel to $CA$ meets $AB$ at $N$. Prove that $$\frac{BL}{LC}\times\frac{CM}{MA}\times\frac{AN}{NB}\leq\frac18$$ and locate the position of $P$ in triangle $ABC$ when equality holds.

uk1.2008.0.6.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2008.0.6.reviewed_statement:
The function $f$ is defined on the set of positive integers by $f(1)=1$, $f(2n)=2f(n)$, and $nf(2n+1)=(2n+1)\big(f(n)+n\big)$ for all $n\geq 1$.
i) Prove that $f(n)$ is always an integer.
ii) For how many positive integers less than $2007$ is $f(n)=2n$?

uk1.2009.0.1.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2009.0.1.reviewed_statement: Consider a standard $8\times 8$ chessboard consisting of $64$ small squares coloured in the usual pattern, so $32$ are black and $32$ are white. A zig-zag path across the board is a collection of eight white squares, one in each row, which meet at their corners. How many zig-zag paths are there?

uk1.2009.0.2.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2009.0.2.reviewed_statement: Find all real values of $x$, $y$ and $z$ such that $$(x+1)yz=12,\qquad (y+1)zx=4\qquad\text{and}\qquad (z+1)xy=4.$$

uk1.2009.0.3.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2009.0.3.reviewed_statement:
Let $ABPC$ be a parallelogram such that $ABC$ is an acute-angled triangle. The circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ meets the line $CP$ again at $Q$. Prove that $PQ=AC$ if, and only if, $\angle BAC=60^\circ$.
The circumcircle of a triangle is the circle which passes through its vertices.

uk1.2009.0.4.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2009.0.4.reviewed_statement: Find all positive integers $n$ such that both $n+2008$ divides $n^2+2008$ and $n+2009$ divides $n^2+2009$.

uk1.2009.0.5.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2009.0.5.reviewed_statement:
Determine the sequences $a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots$ which satisfy all of the following conditions:
a) $a_{n+1}=2a_n^2-1$ for every integer $n\geq 0$,
b) $a_0$ is a rational number and
c) $a_i=a_j$ for some $i$, $j$ with $i\neq j$.

uk1.2009.0.6.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2009.0.6.reviewed_statement: The obtuse-angled triangle $ABC$ has sides of length $a$, $b$ and $c$ opposite the angles $\angle A$, $\angle B$ and $\angle C$ respectively. Prove that $$a^3\cos A+b^3\cos B+c^3\cos C<abc.$$

uk1.2010.0.1.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2010.0.1.reviewed_statement: Find all integers $x$, $y$ and $z$ such that $$x^2+y^2+z^2=2(yz+1)\qquad\text{and}\qquad x+y+z=4018.$$

uk1.2010.0.2.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2010.0.2.reviewed_statement: Points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ and $E$ lie, in that order, on a circle and the lines $AB$ and $ED$ are parallel. Prove that $\angle ABC=90^\circ$ if, and only if, $AC^2=BD^2+CE^2$.

uk1.2010.0.3.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2010.0.3.reviewed_statement: Isaac attempts all six questions on an Olympiad paper in order. Each question is marked on a scale from $0$ to $10$. He never scores more in a later question than in any earlier question. How many different possible sequences of six marks can he achieve?

uk1.2010.0.4.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2010.0.4.reviewed_statement: Two circles, of different radius, with centres at $B$ and $C$, touch externally at $A$. A common tangent, not through $A$, touches the first circle at $D$ and the second at $E$. The line through $A$ which is perpendicular to $DE$ and the perpendicular bisector of $BC$ meet at $F$. Prove that $BC=2AF$.

uk1.2010.0.5.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2010.0.5.reviewed_statement: Find all functions $f$, defined on the real numbers and taking real values, which satisfy the equation $f(x)f(y)=f(x+y)+xy$ for all real numbers $x$ and $y$.

uk1.2010.0.6.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2010.0.6.reviewed_statement: Long John Silverman has captured a treasure map from Adam McBones. Adam has buried the treasure at the point $(x,y)$ with integer co-ordinates (not necessarily positive). He has indicated on the map the values of $x^2+y$ and $x+y^2$, and these numbers are distinct. Prove that Long John has to dig only in one place to find the treasure.

uk1.2011.0.1.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.

Let the tangents to $\Gamma$ at $D$ and $E$ meet at $F$. Suppose that $\angle ACD=\angle ECB$. Prove that $\angle EFD=\angle ACD+\angle ECB$.

uk1.2019.0.5.reviewed_statement: Two solid cylinders are mathematically similar. The sum of their heights is $1$. The sum of their surface areas is $8\pi$. The sum of their volumes is $2\pi$. Find all possibilities for the dimensions of each cylinder.

uk1.2019.0.6.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2019.0.6.reviewed_statement: Ada the ant starts at a point $O$ on a plane. At the start of each minute she chooses North, South, East or West, and marches $1$ metre in that direction. At the end of $2018$ minutes she finds herself back at $O$. Let $n$ be the number of possible journeys which she could have made. What is the highest power of $10$ which divides $n$?

uk1.2020.0.1.reviewed_statement: Show that there are at least three prime numbers $p$ less than 200 for which $p+2$, $p+6$, $p+8$ and $p+12$ are all prime. Show also that there is only one prime number $q$ for which $q+2$, $q+6$, $q+8$, $q+12$ and $q+14$ are all prime.

uk1.2020.0.2.reviewed_statement: A sequence of integers $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ satisfies the relation $4a_{n+1}^2 - 4a_na_{n+1} + a_n^2 - 1 = 0$ for all positive integers $n$. What are the possible values of $a_1$?

uk1.2020.0.3.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2020.0.3.reviewed_statement: Two circles $S_1$ and $S_2$ are tangent at $P$. A common tangent, not through $P$, touches $S_1$ at $A$ and $S_2$ at $B$. Points $C$ and $D$, on $S_1$ and $S_2$ respectively, are outside the triangle $APB$ and are such that $P$ is on the line $CD$. Prove that $AC$ is perpendicular to $BD$.

uk1.2020.0.4.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2020.0.4.reviewed_statement: There are 2019 penguins waddling towards their favourite restaurant. As the penguins arrive, they are handed tickets numbered in ascending order from 1 to 2019, and told to join the queue. The first penguin starts the queue. For each $n > 1$ the penguin holding ticket number $n$ finds the greatest $m < n$ which divides $n$ and enters the queue directly behind the penguin holding ticket number $m$. This continues until all 2019 penguins are in the queue. (a) How many penguins are in front of the penguin with ticket number 2? (b) What numbers are on the tickets held by the penguins just in front of and just behind the penguin holding ticket 33?

uk1.2020.0.5.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2020.0.5.reviewed_statement: Six children are evenly spaced around a circular table. Initially, one has a pile of $n > 0$ sweets in front of them, and the others have nothing. If a child has at least four sweets in front of them, they may perform the following move: eat one sweet and give one sweet to each of their immediate neighbours and to the child directly opposite them. An arrangement is called perfect if there is a sequence of moves which results in each child having the same number of sweets in front of them. For which values of $n$ is the initial arrangement perfect?

uk1.2020.0.6.reviewed_statement: A function $f$ is called good if it assigns an integer value $f(m,n)$ to every ordered pair of integers $(m,n)$ in such a way that for every pair of integers $(m,n)$ we have $$2f(m,n) = f(m-n,\, n-m) + m + n = f(m+1,\, n) + f(m,\, n+1) - 1.$$ Find all good functions.

uk1.2021.0.1.reviewed_statement: [Section A — answer only] Alice and Bob take it in turns to write numbers on a blackboard. Alice starts by writing an integer $a$ between $-100$ and $100$ inclusive on the board. On each of Bob's turns he writes twice the number Alice wrote last. On each of Alice's subsequent turns she writes the number 45 less than the number Bob wrote last. At some point, the number $a$ is written on the board for a second time. Find the possible values of $a$.

uk1.2021.0.2.reviewed_statement: [Section A — answer only] A triangle has side lengths $a$, $a$ and $b$. It has perimeter $P$ and area $A$. Given that $b$ and $P$ are integers, and that $P$ is numerically equal to $A^2$, find all possible pairs $(a,b)$.

uk1.2021.0.3.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2021.0.3.reviewed_statement: [Section A — answer only] A square piece of paper is folded in half along a line of symmetry. The resulting shape is then folded in half along a line of symmetry of the new shape. This process is repeated until $n$ folds have been made, giving a sequence of $n+1$ shapes. If we do not distinguish between congruent shapes, find the number of possible sequences when (a) $n=3$; (b) $n=6$; (c) $n=9$. (When $n=1$ there are two possible sequences.)

uk1.2021.0.4.reviewed_statement: [Section A — answer only] In the equation $$\mathrm{A}^{\mathrm{AA}} + \mathrm{AA} = \mathrm{B,BBC,DED,BEE,BBB,BBE}$$ the letters A, B, C, D and E represent different base 10 digits (so the right hand side is a sixteen digit number and AA is a two digit number). Given that $\mathrm{C} = 9$, find A, B, D and E.

uk1.2021.0.5.reviewed_statement: [Section B] Let points $A$, $B$ and $C$ lie on a circle $\Gamma$. Circle $\Delta$ is tangent to $AC$ at $A$. It meets $\Gamma$ again at $D$ and the line $AB$ again at $P$. The point $A$ lies between points $B$ and $P$. Prove that if $AD = DP$, then $BP = AC$.

uk1.2021.0.6.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2021.0.6.reviewed_statement: [Section B] Given that an integer $n$ is the sum of two different powers of 2 and also the sum of two different Mersenne primes, prove that $n$ is the sum of two different square numbers. (A Mersenne prime is a prime number which is one less than a power of two.)

uk1.2021.0.7.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2021.0.7.reviewed_statement: [Section B] Evie and Odette are playing a game. Three pebbles are placed on the number line; one at $-2020$, one at $2020$, and one at $n$, where $n$ is an integer between $-2020$ and $2020$. They take it in turns moving either the leftmost or the rightmost pebble to an integer between the other two pebbles. The game ends when the pebbles occupy three consecutive integers. Odette wins if their sum is odd; Evie wins if their sum is even. For how many values of $n$ can Evie guarantee victory if (a) Odette goes first; (b) Evie goes first?

uk1.2022.0.1.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2022.0.1.reviewed_statement: Find three even numbers less than 400, each of which can be expressed as a sum of consecutive positive odd numbers in at least six different ways. (Two expressions are considered to be different if they contain different numbers. The order of the numbers forming a sum is irrelevant.)

uk1.2022.0.2.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2022.0.2.reviewed_statement: One day Arun and Disha played several games of table tennis. At five points during the day, Arun calculated the percentage of the games played so far that he had won. The results of these calculations were exactly 30%, exactly 40%, exactly 50%, exactly 60% and exactly 70% in some order. What is the smallest possible number of games they played?

uk1.2022.0.3.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2022.0.3.reviewed_statement: For each integer $0 \le n \le 11$, Eliza has exactly three identical pieces of gold that weigh $2^n$ grams. In how many different ways can she form a pile of gold weighing 2021 grams? (Two piles are different if they contain different numbers of gold pieces of some weight. The arrangement of the pieces in the piles is irrelevant.)

uk1.2022.0.4.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2022.0.4.reviewed_statement: Two circles $\Gamma_1$ and $\Gamma_2$ have centres $O_1$ and $O_2$ respectively. They pass through each other's centres and intersect at $A$ and $B$. The point $C$ lies on the minor arc $BO_2$ of $\Gamma_1$. The points $D$ and $E$ lie on the line $O_2C$ such that $\angle AO_1D = \angle DO_1C$ and $\angle CO_1E = \angle EO_1B$. Prove that triangle $DO_1E$ is equilateral. (A minor arc of a circle is the shorter of the two arcs with given endpoints.)

uk1.2022.0.5.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2022.0.5.reviewed_statement: An $N$-set is a set of different positive integers including a given positive integer $N$. Let $m(N)$ be the smallest possible mean of any $N$-set. For how many values of $N$ less than 2021 is $m(N)$ an integer?

uk1.2022.0.6.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2022.0.6.reviewed_statement: Marvin has been tasked with writing down every list of integers with the following properties: (i) the list contains 71 terms; (ii) the first term is 1; (iii) every term after the first is equal to either the previous term, or the sum of all previous terms. When Marvin is finished, how many of the lists will have a sum equal to 999,999?

uk1.2023.0.1.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2023.0.1.reviewed_statement: A road has houses numbered from 1 to $n$, where $n$ is a three-digit number. Exactly $\frac{1}{k}$ of the numbers start with the digit 2, where $k$ is a positive integer. Find the possible values of $n$.

uk1.2023.0.2.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2023.0.2.reviewed_statement: A sequence of positive integers $a_n$ begins with $a_1 = a$ and $a_2 = b$ for positive integers $a$ and $b$. Subsequent terms in the sequence satisfy the following two rules for all positive integers $n$: $$a_{2n+1} = a_{2n}a_{2n-1}, \qquad a_{2n+2} = a_{2n+1} + 4.$$ Exactly $m$ of the numbers $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots, a_{2022}$ are square numbers. What is the maximum possible value of $m$? Note that $m$ depends on $a$ and $b$, so the maximum is over all possible choices of $a$ and $b$.

uk1.2023.0.3.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2023.0.3.reviewed_statement: In an acute, non-isosceles triangle $ABC$ the midpoints of $AC$ and $AB$ are $B_1$ and $C_1$ respectively. A point $D$ lies on $BC$ with $C$ between $B$ and $D$. The point $F$ is such that $\angle AFC$ is a right angle and $\angle DCF = \angle FCA$. The point $G$ is such that $\angle AGB$ is a right angle and $\angle CBG = \angle GBA$. Prove that $B_1$, $C_1$, $F$ and $G$ are collinear.

uk1.2023.0.4.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2023.0.4.reviewed_statement: Alex and Katy play a game on an $8 \times 8$ square grid made of 64 unit cells. They take it in turns to play, with Alex going first. On Alex's turn, he writes 'A' in an empty cell. On Katy's turn, she writes 'K' in two empty cells that share an edge. The game ends when one player cannot move. Katy's score is the number of Ks on the grid at the end of the game. What is the highest score Katy can be sure to get if she plays well, no matter what Alex does?

uk1.2023.0.5.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2023.0.5.reviewed_statement: For each integer $n \ge 1$, let $f(n)$ be the number of lists of different positive integers starting with 1 and ending with $n$, in which each term except the last divides its successor. Prove that for each integer $N \ge 1$ there is an integer $n \ge 1$ such that $N$ divides $f(n)$. (So $f(1)=1$, $f(2)=1$ and $f(6)=3$.)

uk1.2023.0.6.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2023.0.6.reviewed_statement: A circle $\Gamma$ has radius 1. A line $l$ is such that the perpendicular distance from $l$ to the centre of $\Gamma$ is strictly between 0 and 2. A frog chooses a point on $\Gamma$ whose perpendicular distance from $l$ is less than 1 and sits on that point. It then performs a sequence of jumps. Each jump has length 1 and if a jump starts on $\Gamma$ it must end on $l$ and vice versa. Prove that after some finite number of jumps the frog returns to a point it has been on before.

uk1.2024.0.1.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2024.0.1.reviewed_statement: An unreliable typist can guarantee that when they try to type a word with different letters, every letter of the word will appear exactly once in what they type, and each letter will occur at most one letter late (though it may occur more than one letter early). Thus, when trying to type MATHS, the typist may type MATHS, MTAHS or TMASH, but not ATMSH. Determine, with proof, the number of possible spellings of OLYMPIADS that might be typed.

uk1.2024.0.2.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2024.0.2.reviewed_statement: The sequence of integers $a_0, a_1, \dots$ has the property that for each $i \ge 2$, $a_i$ is either $2a_{i-1} - a_{i-2}$ or $2a_{i-2} - a_{i-1}$. Given that $a_{2023}$ and $a_{2024}$ are consecutive integers, prove that $a_0$ and $a_1$ are consecutive integers. (Note that 6 and 7 are consecutive integers, as are 7 and 6.)

uk1.2024.0.3.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2024.0.3.reviewed_statement: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle ACB < \angle BAC < 90^\circ$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be points on $AC$ and the circle $ABC$ respectively such that $X, Y \ne A$ and $BX = BY = BA$. Line $XY$ intersects the circle $ABC$ again at $Z$. Prove that $BZ$ is perpendicular to $AC$.

uk1.2024.0.4.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2024.0.4.reviewed_statement: Find all positive integers $n$ such that $n \times 2^n + 1$ is a square.

uk1.2024.0.5.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2024.0.5.reviewed_statement: An artist arranges 1000 dots evenly around a circle, with each dot being either red or blue. A critic looks at the artwork and counts faults: each time two red dots are adjacent is one fault, and each time two blue dots are exactly two apart (that is, they have exactly one dot in between them) is another. What is the smallest number of faults the critic could find?

uk1.2024.0.6.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2024.0.6.reviewed_statement: For some integer $n > 4$ a convex polygon has vertices $v_1, v_2, \dots, v_n$ in that cyclic order. All its edges are the same length. It also has the property that the lengths of the diagonals $v_1v_4, v_2v_5, \dots, v_{n-3}v_n, v_{n-2}v_1, v_{n-1}v_2$ and $v_nv_3$ are all equal. For which $n$ is it necessarily the case that the polygon has equal angles?

uk1.2025.0.1.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2025.0.1.reviewed_statement: We say that the positive integer $n \ge 3$ is happy if it is possible to arrange $n$ different positive integers in a circle such that two conditions are satisfied: (a) if integers $u$ and $v$ in the circle are neighbours, then either $u$ divides $v$ or $v$ divides $u$; (b) if different integers $u$ and $v$ are in the circle but are not neighbours, then neither divides the other. Determine, with proof, which positive integers $n$ in the range $3 \le n \le 12$ are happy.

uk1.2025.0.2.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2025.0.2.reviewed_statement: A magician performs a trick with a deck of $n$ cards that are numbered from 1 to $n$. The magician prepares for the trick by putting the cards in an order of her choosing. Then she challenges a member of the audience to write an integer on a board. The magician turns over the cards one by one, in their pre-arranged order. Every time the magician turns over a card, the audience member multiplies the number on the board by $-1$, adds it to the number on the card, writes the result on the board, and erases the old number. The magician guarantees that, no matter which initial integer is chosen, the initial and final numbers will sum to 0. Determine for which natural numbers $n$ the magician can perform the trick. You must both prove that the trick is possible for the numbers you claim, and prove that it is not possible for any other numbers.

uk1.2025.0.3.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2025.0.3.reviewed_statement: Rhian and Jack are playing a game in which initially the number $10^6$ is written on a blackboard. If the current number on the board is $n$, a move consists of choosing two different positive integers $a, b$ such that $n = ab$ and replacing $n$ with $|a-b|$. Rhian starts, then the players make moves alternately. A player loses if they are unable to move. Determine, with proof, which player has a winning strategy.

uk1.2025.0.4.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2025.0.4.reviewed_statement: In the acute-angled triangle $ABC$ we have $AB < AC < BC$. The midpoint of $BC$ is $M$. There is a point $P$ on the line segment $AM$ such that $AB = CP$, and $\angle PAB = \angle BCP$. Prove that $\angle CPB = 90^\circ$.

uk1.2025.0.5.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2025.0.5.reviewed_statement: Let $p$ be a prime number, and let $n$ be the smallest positive integer, strictly greater than 1, for which $n^6 - 1$ is divisible by $p$. Prove that at least one of $(n+1)^6 - 1$ and $(n+2)^6 - 1$ is divisible by $p$.

uk1.2025.0.6.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2025.0.6.reviewed_statement: Björk has 64 sugar cubes, all of size $1 \times 1 \times 1$. Each sugar cube is either white or demerara or muscovado in flavour. She piles the sugar cubes into a neat $4 \times 4 \times 4$ cube. Prove that there must be 12 sugar cubes of the same flavour which can be put into 6 disjoint pairs so that the distance between the centres of the cubes in each pair is the same.

uk1.2026.0.1.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2026.0.1.reviewed_statement: A ramp is a sequence of three different positive integers $a, b, c$ such that $a$ is a factor of $b$ and $b$ is a factor of $c$. For every prime number $p$ and every positive integer $n$, determine with proof whether $p^n$ can be expressed as the sum of a ramp.

uk1.2026.0.2.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2026.0.2.reviewed_statement: Find all triples $(x, y, z)$ of real numbers satisfying the equations $$x^2 + 2yz = 4, \qquad y^2 + 2zx = 4, \qquad z^2 + 2xy = 1.$$

uk1.2026.0.3.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2026.0.3.reviewed_statement: An $11 \times 11$ square grid is dissected into 11 pieces as follows. At each step, remove the top row and the leftmost column of the remaining grid as a single piece. Thus, the pieces obtained are L-shaped with sizes $21, 19, \dots, 3$, together with a single square. The pieces are rearranged to reassemble an $11 \times 11$ grid, with rotations allowed (but the pieces may not be turned over) so that the single square occupies the cell in the third row and third column (counting from the top left). How many ways can this be done?

The circle passing through $M$ that is tangent to $AB$ at $B$ and the circle passing through $M$ that is tangent to $AC$ at $C$ intersect again at $D$. Prove that $MA \times MD = MB \times MC$.

uk1.2026.0.5.reviewed_statement: George defines a sequence of positive integers $t_1, t_2, t_3, \dots$ as follows. He first sets $t_1 = 1$. Then, for $n \ge 1$: if $t_n$ is even, then $t_{n+1} = t_n/2$; if $t_n$ is odd and greater than 1, then $t_{n+1}$ is $t_n/3$ rounded to the nearest integer; if $t_n = 1$, then $t_{n+1} = 2025k$, where $k$ is the number of terms equal to 1 amongst $t_1, t_2, \dots, t_n$. Does this sequence contain every positive integer?

uk1.2026.0.6.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk1.2026.0.6.reviewed_statement: There are 1000 lily pads on a pond arranged in a circle and labelled $1, 2, \dots, 1000$ in order. (The first four lily pads may also be described using the labels 1001, 1002, 1003 and 1004, respectively.) The first $n$ lily pads are each occupied by a frog with the remaining lily pads not occupied. Each minute, exactly one of the frogs makes a move. Suppose the frog is on lily pad $k$. That frog may either (i) swim to lily pad $k+4$ or $k-4$, provided that it is not occupied; or (ii) jump to lily pad $k+3$ or $k-3$, provided that this lily pad is not occupied and the two lily pads jumped over are both occupied. When this happens, the two frogs that were jumped over dive into the pond and don't participate in any further moves. For which values of $n$ is it possible, by a sequence of moves, to end with exactly one frog remaining on the lily pads?

uk2.2006.0.2.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.

uk2.2006.0.3.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.

uk2.2006.0.4.reviewed_statement: An exam consisting of six questions is sat by 2006 children. Each question is marked either right or wrong. Find the least possible value of $N$.

uk2.2007.0.1.reviewed_statement: Triangle $ABC$ has integer-length sides, and $AC = 2007$. The internal bisector of $\angle BAC$ meets $BC$ at $D$. Given that $AB = CD$, determine $AB$ and $BC$.

uk2.2007.0.2.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk2.2007.0.2.reviewed_statement: Show that there are infinitely many pairs of positive integers $(m, n)$ such that $$\frac{m+1}{n} + \frac{n+1}{m}$$ is a positive integer.

uk2.2007.0.3.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk2.2007.0.3.reviewed_statement:
Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB > AC$ and $\angle BAC = 60^\circ$. Denote the circumcentre by $O$ and the orthocentre by $H$ and let $OH$ meet $AB$ at $P$ and $AC$ at $Q$. Prove that $PO = HQ$.

uk2.2007.0.4.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk2.2007.0.4.reviewed_statement: In the land of Hexagonia, the six cities are connected by a rail network such that there is a direct rail line connecting each pair of cities. On Sundays, some lines may be closed for repair. The passengers' rail charter stipulates that any city must be accessible by rail from any other (not necessarily directly) at all times. In how many different ways can some of the lines be closed subject to this condition?

uk2.2008.0.1.reviewed_statement: Find the minimum value of $x^2 + y^2 + z^2$ where $x, y, z$ are real numbers such that $x^3 + y^3 + z^3 - 3xyz = 1$.

uk2.2008.0.2.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk2.2008.0.2.reviewed_statement: Let triangle $ABC$ have incentre $I$ and circumcentre $O$. Suppose that $\angle AIO = 90^\circ$ and $\angle CIO = 45^\circ$. Find the ratio $AB : BC : CA$.

uk2.2008.0.3.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk2.2008.0.3.reviewed_statement: Adrian has drawn a circle in the $xy$-plane whose radius is a positive integer at most 2008. The origin lies somewhere inside the circle. You are allowed to ask him questions of the form "Is the point $(x, y)$ inside your circle?" After each question he will answer truthfully "yes" or "no". Show that it is always possible to deduce the radius of the circle after at most sixty questions. [Note: Any point which lies exactly on the circle may be considered to lie inside the circle.]

uk2.2008.0.4.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk2.2008.0.4.reviewed_statement: Prove that there are infinitely many pairs of distinct positive integers $x, y$ such that $x^2 + y^3$ is divisible by $x^3 + y^2$.

uk2.2009.0.1.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk2.2009.0.1.reviewed_statement: Find all solutions in non-negative integers $a, b$ to $\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b} = \sqrt{2009}$.

uk2.2009.0.2.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk2.2009.0.2.reviewed_statement:
Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $\angle B = \angle C$. Let the circumcentre be $O$ and the orthocentre be $H$. Prove that the centre of the circle $BOH$ lies on the line $AB$.
The circumcentre of a triangle is the centre of its circumcircle. The orthocentre of a triangle is the point where its three altitudes meet.

uk2.2009.0.3.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk2.2009.0.3.reviewed_statement: Find all functions $f$ from the real numbers to the real numbers which satisfy $$f(x^3) + f(y^3) = (x+y)\left(f(x^2) + f(y^2) - f(xy)\right)$$ for all real numbers $x$ and $y$.

uk2.2009.0.4.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk2.2009.0.4.reviewed_statement: Given a positive integer $n$, let $b(n)$ denote the number of positive integers whose binary representations occur as blocks of consecutive integers in the binary expansion of $n$. For example $b(13) = 6$ because $13 = 1101_2$, which contains as consecutive blocks the binary representations of $13 = 1101_2$, $6 = 110_2$, $5 = 101_2$, $3 = 11_2$, $2 = 10_2$ and $1 = 1_2$. Show that if $n \le 2500$, then $b(n) \le 39$, and determine the values of $n$ for which equality holds.

uk2.2010.0.1.reviewed_statement: There are $2010^{2010}$ children at a mathematics camp. Each has at most three friends at the camp, and if $A$ is friends with $B$, then $B$ is friends with $A$. The camp leader would like to line the children up so that there are at most 2010 children between any pair of friends. Is it always possible to do this?

uk2.2010.0.2.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk2.2010.0.2.reviewed_statement:
In triangle $ABC$ the centroid is $G$ and $D$ is the midpoint of $CA$. The line through $G$ parallel to $BC$ meets $AB$ at $E$. Prove that $\angle AEC = \angle DGC$ if, and only if, $\angle ACB = 90^\circ$.
The centroid of a triangle is the intersection of the three medians, the lines which join each vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.

uk2.2010.0.3.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk2.2010.0.3.reviewed_statement: The integer $x$ is at least 3 and $n = x^6 - 1$. Let $p$ be a prime and $k$ be a positive integer such that $p^k$ is a factor of $n$. Show that $p^{3k} < 8n$.

uk2.2010.0.4.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk2.2010.0.4.reviewed_statement: Prove that, for all positive real numbers $x$, $y$ and $z$, $$4(x+y+z)^3 > 27(x^2y + y^2z + z^2x).$$

uk2.2011.0.1.reviewed_statement: Let $ABC$ be a triangle and $X$ be a point inside the triangle. The lines $AX$, $BX$ and $CX$ meet the circle $ABC$ again at $P$, $Q$ and $R$ respectively. Choose a point $U$ on $XP$ which is between $X$ and $P$. Suppose that the lines through $U$ which are parallel to $AB$ and $CA$ meet $XQ$ and $XR$ at points $V$ and $W$ respectively. Prove that the points $R$, $W$, $V$ and $Q$ lie on a circle.

uk2.2011.0.2.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk2.2011.0.2.reviewed_statement: Find all positive integers $x$ and $y$ such that $x + y + 1$ divides $2xy$ and $x + y - 1$ divides $x^2 + y^2 - 1$.

uk2.2011.0.3.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk2.2011.0.3.reviewed_statement: The function $f$ is defined on the positive integers as follows: $f(1) = 1$; $f(2n) = f(n)$ if $n$ is even; $f(2n) = 2f(n)$ if $n$ is odd; $f(2n+1) = 2f(n) + 1$ if $n$ is even; $f(2n+1) = f(n)$ if $n$ is odd. Find the number of positive integers $n$ which are less than 2011 and have the property that $f(n) = f(2011)$.

uk2.2011.0.4.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk2.2011.0.4.reviewed_statement: Let $G$ be the set of points $(x, y)$ in the plane such that $x$ and $y$ are integers in the range $1 \le x, y \le 2011$. A subset $S$ of $G$ is said to be parallelogram-free if there is no proper parallelogram with all its vertices in $S$. Determine the largest possible size of a parallelogram-free subset of $G$. Note that a proper parallelogram is one where its vertices do not all lie on the same line.

uk2.2012.0.1.reviewed_statement: The diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ of a cyclic quadrilateral meet at $E$. The midpoints of the sides $AB$, $BC$, $CD$ and $DA$ are $P$, $Q$, $R$ and $S$ respectively. Prove that the circles $EPS$ and $EQR$ have the same radius.

uk2.2012.0.2.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk2.2012.0.2.reviewed_statement:
A function $f$ is defined on the positive integers by $f(1) = 1$ and, for $n > 1$, $$f(n) = f\left(\left\lfloor \frac{2n-1}{3} \right\rfloor\right) + f\left(\left\lfloor \frac{2n}{3} \right\rfloor\right),$$ where $\lfloor x \rfloor$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$. Is it true that $f(n) - f(n-1) \le n$ for all $n > 1$?
[Here are some examples of the use of $\lfloor x\rfloor$: $\lfloor\pi\rfloor=3$, $\lfloor 1729\rfloor=1729$ and $\lfloor\frac{2012}{1000}\rfloor=2$.]

uk2.2012.0.3.reviewed_statement: The set of real numbers is split into two subsets which do not intersect. Prove that for each pair $(m, n)$ of positive integers, there are real numbers $x < y < z$ all in the same subset such that $m(z - y) = n(y - x)$.

uk2.2013.0.1.reviewed_statement: Are there infinitely many pairs of positive integers $(m, n)$ such that both $m$ divides $n^2 + 1$ and $n$ divides $m^2 + 1$?

uk2.2014.0.1.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk2.2014.0.1.reviewed_statement: Every diagonal of a regular polygon with 2014 sides is coloured in one of $n$ colours. Whenever two diagonals cross in the interior, they are of different colours. What is the minimum value of $n$ for which this is possible?

uk2.2014.0.2.reviewed_statement: Prove that it is impossible to have a cuboid for which the volume, the surface area and the perimeter are numerically equal. The perimeter of a cuboid is the sum of the lengths of all its twelve edges.

uk2.2014.0.3.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk2.2014.0.3.reviewed_statement: Let $a_0 = 4$ and define a sequence of terms using the formula $a_n = a_{n-1}^2 - a_{n-1}$ for each positive integer $n$. (a) Prove that there are infinitely many prime numbers which are factors of at least one term in the sequence. (b) Are there infinitely many prime numbers which are factors of no term in the sequence?

uk2.2014.0.4.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk2.2014.0.4.reviewed_statement: Let $ABC$ be a triangle and $P$ be a point in its interior. Let $AP$ meet the circumcircle of $ABC$ again at $A'$. The points $B'$ and $C'$ are similarly defined. Let $O_A$ be the circumcentre of $BCP$. The circumcentres $O_B$ and $O_C$ are similarly defined. Let $O_{A'}$ be the circumcentre of $B'C'P$. The circumcentres $O_{B'}$ and $O_{C'}$ are similarly defined. Prove that the lines $O_AO_{A'}$, $O_BO_{B'}$ and $O_CO_{C'}$ are concurrent.

uk2.2015.0.1.reviewed_statement: The first term $x_1$ of a sequence is 2014. Each subsequent term of the sequence is defined in terms of the previous term. The iterative formula is $$x_{n+1} = \frac{(\sqrt{2}+1)x_n - 1}{(\sqrt{2}+1) + x_n}.$$ Find the 2015th term $x_{2015}$.

One pupil from each class will be chosen to form the school council. Prove that the following two statements are logically equivalent. (a) There are more ways to form a school council which includes an odd number of boys than ways to form a school council which includes an odd number of girls. (b) There are an odd number of classes which contain more boys than girls.

uk2.2015.0.3.reviewed_statement: Two circles touch one another internally at $A$. A variable chord $PQ$ of the outer circle touches the inner circle. Prove that the locus of the incentre of triangle $AQP$ is another circle touching the given circles at $A$. (The incentre of a triangle is the centre of the unique circle which is inside the triangle and touches all three sides. A locus is the collection of all points which satisfy a given condition.)

uk2.2015.0.4.scope: Full statement compared with the official UKMT paper (bmos.ukmt.org.uk; file year = year of the summer term, e.g. bmo1-2005 is the paper of 1 December 2004), by text and on the page image.
uk2.2015.0.4.reviewed_statement: Given two points $P$ and $Q$ with integer coordinates, we say that $P$ sees $Q$ if the line segment $PQ$ contains no other points with integer coordinates. An $n$-loop is a sequence of $n$ points $P_1, P_2, \dots, P_n$, each with integer coordinates, such that the following conditions hold: (a) $P_i$ sees $P_{i+1}$ for $1 \le i \le n-1$, and $P_n$ sees $P_1$; (b) no $P_i$ sees any $P_j$ apart from those mentioned in (a); (c) no three of the points lie on the same straight line. Does there exist a 100-loop?

Consider the sequence $a_1, a_2, \dots$ defined by $$a_n = \frac{1}{n}\left(\left\lfloor \frac{n}{1} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor \frac{n}{2} \right\rfloor + \cdots + \left\lfloor \frac{n}{n} \right\rfloor\right)$$ for integers $n \ge 1$. Prove that $a_{n+1} > a_n$ for infinitely many $n$, and determine whether $a_{n+1} < a_n$ for infinitely many $n$.
[Here are some examples of the use of $\lfloor x\rfloor$: $\lfloor\pi\rfloor=3$, $\lfloor 1729\rfloor=1729$ and $\lfloor\frac{2017}{1000}\rfloor=2$.]

In fact the Mad Hatter is very bossy, and tells Alice that, for $i = 1, 2, \dots, n-1$, when she moves for the $i$-th time, she must move $a_i$ places, and he hands Alice the list of instructions $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{n-1}$. Alice does not like the cakes, and she is free to choose, at every stage, whether to move clockwise or anticlockwise. For which values of $n$ can the Mad Hatter force Alice to eat all the cakes?

(b) Does there exist an absorbing function $f$ and an increasing sequence of real numbers $a_1 < a_2 < a_3 < \cdots$ such that $f(x)$ is an integer only if $x = a_i$ for some $i$? (Note: if $k$ is a positive integer and $f$ is a function, then $f^k$ denotes the composition of $k$ copies of $f$; for example $f^3(t) = f(f(f(t)))$ for all real numbers $t$.)

uk2.2026.0.3.reviewed_statement: Each cell of a $30 \times 30$ grid contains one of the numbers $-1$, $0$ or $1$, with each of these three numbers appearing exactly 300 times. Is it possible that the 60 row and column sums are all different?

uk2.2026.0.4.reviewed_statement: Let $N$ be a positive integer and let $(k_n)_{n \ge 1}$ be a sequence of positive integers with all terms at most $N$. Annabel begins by choosing integers $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_N$. She then extends this to an infinite sequence $(x_n)_{n \ge 1}$ of integers by defining $$x_n = \sum_{i=n-k_n}^{n-1} x_i$$ for each $n > N$. Show that there are either finitely many strictly positive terms or finitely many strictly negative terms in the infinite sequence $(x_n)$.
